meeting_header:
Date: 2025-07-22
Time: 10:00 AM - 10:34 AM PDT
Duration: 34 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood CSM); Maya Thompson (Crestview Head of Data), Owen Li (ML Eng), Samira Khan (Security), Ben Park (Product)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review quality evaluation results across the pilot prompt sets, discuss regressions, tune guardrails and outline next steps for latency benchmarking and security follow-up. Agreement to iterate on scoring rubric, run a dedicated-latency benchmark, and clarify SOC2/KMS questions.
topics: Eval results overview (precision/recall and hallucination rate)
Prompt set regressions and guardrail failures
Scoring rubric adjustments and threshold for go/no-go
transcript:
00:00 Sarah (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
00:07 Maya (Crestview): Hi, Maya here.
00:09 Owen: Owen.
00:10 Samira: Samira.
00:11 Ben: Ben here.
00:13 Diego (Redwood SE): Diego, hey.
00:15 Priya (Redwood CSM): Priya on for notes.
00:18 Sarah: Great, agenda: run through last week's quality eval, highlight any regressions, discuss guardrails, and confirm next steps. Owen you had pre-shared the false-positive examples so we'll start there.
00:34 Owen: Yeah, thanks. So we ran your prompt set A and B across the 5k sample we agreed on. Summary numbers are in the sheet, but topline: precision down ~6% on A week-over-week, hallucination rate up — especially on clinical-summarization prompts.
00:52 Sarah: Ok, do you mean the model is inventing diagnoses or adding incorrect medication names?
00:57 Owen: Mostly invented small details — dates, sometimes med names that look plausible but are wrong.
01:05 Diego: That's consistent with what we saw when we swapped quantization profiles. We think one of the quantized variants is dropping some token fidelity in rare subword sequences which can flip clinical tokens.
01:18 Samira: That ties to our security risk assessment — hallucinations in PHI contexts are high risk. We need guardrails and deterministic post-checks.
01:27 Sarah: Understood. Quick sanity: which model/variant produced the worse numbers? (A vs B, hosted vs ded?).
01:33 Owen: 1) Hosted on latest rdx-llm-3-quant produced most hallucinations. 2) Dedicated 16-bit run was slightly better, but still not ideal.
01:45 Diego: Right — and small detail: the hosted run used the auto-quant path. The dedicated run used the non-quant 16-bit. The auto path sometimes switches to 4-bit for token perf and that's likely the regression vector.
02:00 Ben: Is auto-quant something we can control? It sounds like a hidden toggler.
02:04 Diego: You can pin quant profile in the deployment config. We can force 16-bit or a conservative quant profile for critical prompts.
02:11 Maya: If we lose performance, that could break latency SLOs for the patient-facing tool. We need a balance.
02:18 Sarah: Good — tradeoff conversation coming. Let's dig into a couple of concrete examples from the sheet. Owen, can you read one?
02:25 Owen: Sure, example #342: input was a discharge summary; model inserted "history of pernicious anemia" incorrectly. The ground truth didn't have that.
02:35 Diego: That's the subword fidelity issue — pernicious/ per-ni-cious tokenization sometimes collapses with quant noise.
02:43 Priya: Note: transcript—sorry — note: several of these examples failed the current guardrail because the defensive regex didn't catch alternate spellings.
02:52 Samira: For compliance, we need explicit deterministic filters for any PHI change — e.g., block model from outputting novel diagnoses unless verified by a human.
03:03 Sarah: Could we add a classification step post-generation? Like a quick hallucination detector?
03:07 Diego: Yes, you can run a lightweight classifier against generation; Redwood Optimize suggests an ensemble approach: prefix-check + hallucination classifier + hard guardrail. But that adds latency.
03:20 Ben: How much?
03:22 Diego: Depends. On our infra a binary classifier adds ~30-50ms p99 on dedicated, could be 80-120ms on hosted depending on routing.
03:31 Maya: 80-120ms might be acceptable if it's targeted to critical endpoints only.
03:35 Sarah: Actionable: we'll mark which prompt families need the classifier.
03:38 Owen: Quick note on scoring: the current rubric weights precision 70/30 with recall; we think that undervalues safety. I propose shifting to 60/40 precision/recall and adding hallucination penalty.
03:52 Sarah: Happy to try that. Diego, can you re-run the scoring with the new weights?
03:56 Diego: Yep — I'll update the eval script and re-score. Expect results in next spreadsheet iteration.
04:03 Priya: Also to call out, some of the 'false positives' are actually extraction errors where the model combined nearby phrases. Might be fixable via prompt engineering rather than model change.
04:15 Owen: Agreed. We have a small set of prompts that when rephrased drop hallucinations. We'll send candidates.
04:22 Sarah: Perfect.
04:25 Sarah: On the regression — do we want to pin to a non-auto-quant variant for the pilot? Or do we accept a slower hosted path?
04:33 Ben: Cost matters. If dedicated reduces hallucination but costs 3x, procurement will push back.
04:39 Samira: For regulated flows we prefer dedicated with KMS integration so keys never leave our VPC.
04:46 Diego: We can propose a hybrid: dedicated for PII/clinical pathways, hosted for low-risk tasks. Redwood routing can split by route with fallbacks.
04:55 Maya: That could work. We need to measure latency differential for both.
04:58 Sarah: Diego, you suggested a dedicated benchmark. Can you outline what you'll run?
05:04 Diego: I'll run a 1k synchronous request workload across: hosted auto-quant, dedicated 16-bit, and dedicated 8-bit quant profile pinned. We'll measure p50/p90/p99 latency and cost per 1k tokens. I'll use your representative prompt family and the exact token lengths from the sample.
05:21 Owen: Important to include KV cache warm/cold runs — some of our app flows will have long conversations.
05:28 Diego: Good call, I'll include cold start and steady-state.
05:31 Priya: Also include streaming vs non-streamed response; the patient UI uses streaming.
05:36 Diego: Noted.
05:38 Samira: On compliance, we had a few SOC2/KMS follow-ups. Who owns clarifying whether Redwood's private deployment supports HSM-backed keys?
05:46 Sarah: That's on me. I'll check with infra and legal. My read: Redwood Private supports customer KMS and HSM integration for on-prem; we'll confirm product notes and share the diagram.
05:56 Samira: Please specify encryption at rest, key rotation policy, and audit log retention in the follow-up.
06:02 Sarah: Will do.
06:03 Ben: Any blockers on data residency? Some patients are in EU.
06:07 Sarah: We have EU regions in private/dedicated — we'll map that.
06:11 Maya: Awesome.
06:13 Owen: Back to guardrails: a couple of prompts triggered the 'allowed-entities' guardrail but the entity list wasn't exhaustive, so model slipped in other entity types.
06:22 Diego: We can make the guardrail fuzzy-match aware and add a deny-list for sensitive tokens. Also a post-check to redact novel medical-sounding tokens pending human review.
06:31 Samira: Redaction is acceptable as a stop-gap, but we need human-in-the-loop for final clinical text before it hits patient records.
06:38 Sarah: For the POC success criteria, let's document: 1) Hallucination rate under X% for clinical-critical prompts (TBD), 2) Latency under 400ms p90 for patient UI flows, 3) Ability to enforce KMS/HSM controls for private data. Agree?
06:53 Maya: Sounds right but we need exact X. Owen, can you suggest a threshold from the eval?
06:58 Owen: Based on distribution I'd recommend <2% hallucination on critical prompts; with current it's at ~4.8% on A.
07:07 Diego: If we pin quant to 16-bit I think we can get to ~2.2-2.5%.
07:13 Ben: That might be acceptable if we have human review on edge cases.
07:16 Sarah: Ok, add that to next steps.
07:19 Priya: Quick logistics: we'll share an updated scoring sheet. Also include a column for whether remediation is prompt-engineering, model config, or guardrail.
07:29 Owen: We'll label examples accordingly.
07:31 Sarah: Any other customer-side asks?
07:34 Samira: Please share SOC2 docs and a diagram of private deployment network flow.
07:38 Sarah: Yep, will send.
07:40 Ben: Can Redwood provide a TCO estimate for dedicated if we scale to 10k monthly active users? That helps procurement.
07:47 Diego: We can produce a ballpark based on tokens/sec and instance sizing; I'll work with pricing to generate a calc.
07:53 Sarah: I'll include it in the follow-up.
07:55 Maya: One more: how do auto-rollbacks work if a new model variant starts producing regressions? We saw that in another vendor.
08:03 Diego: Redwood has rollout policies: canary, automatic rollback on metric regressions tied to eval hooks. We'll share the docs. Automatic rollback can be configured for quality regressions and latency spikes.
08:16 Sarah: Ok wrapping up. Recap of next steps: Sarah send eval sheet + SOC2/KMS answers; Diego run dedicated benchmarks; Maya/Owen provide final prompt list & sensitive fields; Samira share compliance Qs. We'll reconvene next Tuesday same time.
08:34 Priya: I'll create a calendar invite for the deep-dive on 2025-07-29.
08:38 Sarah: Thanks everyone.
08:40 Owen: Thanks.
08:42 Samira: Thanks all.
08:44 (call ends)

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts present (product names like "rdx" or "Reedwood" mentioned in quick chat). References: eval spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.app/crested-eval/2025-07-22), SOC2 overview doc (link shared post-call).
